BATTLEGROUND I: THE PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT
EXTREME
OPPOSITION
The Mensheviks argue that joining a provisional
government sanctifies the bourgeois order
(Millerandism). They choose to remain an
extreme revolutionary opposition exerting
pressure only from below.
The Bolsheviks argue that abstaining tolerates the
putrid autocracy. They demand pressure from both
below and above, using the provisional
revolutionary government as an organ of the
insurrection to ruthlessly crush counter-revolution.

THE ILLUSION OF PARLIAMENTARY TACTICS
The Mensheviks adopt the slogan of extreme opposition-a concept built for peaceful
parliamentary democracies. Lenin exposes this absurdity: You cannot simply vote
against, expose, or refuse funds to a government when civil war has already begun.
School exercises in parliamentarism are useless when the bayonet is on the agenda.

BATTLEGROUND I: ARMED INSURRECTION
ZEMSKY SOBOR
Menshevik Delusion: Waiting to split the deputies.
Bolshevik Tactic: Planned organization and active arming.
The Menshevik Conference treats the Bulgin Zemsky Sobor (a promised, powerless tsarist assembly) as the center of action.
Lenin ridicules this parliamentary cretinism. The autocracy is stalling to consolidate power. The only correct tactic is to
actively arm the proletariat and plan the insurrection, rather than waiting for spontaneous socio-psychological conditions.

THE REVOLUTIONARY COMMUNES EVASION
Realizing the absurdity of rejecting power entirely, the Mensheviks concede to forming episodic,
local revolutionary communes to disrupt the government. Lenin identifies this as revolutionary
phrase-mongering. Evoking the Paris Commune is a historical error that confuses democratic and
and socialist tasks. Seizing power in one city inevitably requires administering state affairs;
evading a national Provisional Government is a dereliction of duty.

DARE WE WIN?
The defining feature of the intellectual-opportunist wing of the party is the fear of victory.
Martynov and the New-Iskraists write resolutions warning that the party might be discredited if it
seizes power and cannot immediately deliver socialism. Lenin demands an end to this cowardice.
An army cannot be successfully mustered if its leaders are terrified of actually winning the battle.

THE LOCOMOTIVES
OF HISTORY
Revolutions are the festivals of
the oppressed and the exploited.
In stormy times, the advanced class must discard the narrow, philistine scale of
gradual progress. The party's duty is not to invent circuitous, roundabout paths
out of fear, but to provide the beacons and slogans that lead the masses along
the most direct route to complete and absolute victory.
